theory.overview: While vanilla gradient descent works, modern deep learning relies on sophisticated optimizers that adapt learning rates per-parameter and incorporate momentum. These algorithms—RMSprop, AdaGrad, and especially Adam—solve real problems: some parameters need bigger updates than others, gradients vary wildly across dimensions, and we want to escape saddle points quickly. Understanding these optimizers helps you train faster, converge better, and achieve state-of-the-art results.

sections.title: The Problem: One Size Doesn't Fit All
sections.content: In deep networks, different layers and parameters have vastly different gradient scales. Early layers (detecting edges in images) need different updates than late layers (classifying objects). Sparse features (rare words) need larger updates than frequent ones. A single global learning rate is suboptimal—some parameters need speed, others need caution.
sections.example: In word embeddings, the word 'the' appears constantly—its embedding needs tiny updates. 'Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis' appears once—its embedding needs a big update.

sections.title: AdaGrad: Per-Parameter Learning Rates
sections.content: AdaGrad accumulates squared gradients for each parameter, then divides the learning rate by the square root of this sum. Frequently updated parameters get smaller effective learning rates; rarely updated ones get larger rates.
cons: Learning rate monotonically decreases—eventually stops learning
Aggressive decay can be too strong

sections.title: RMSprop: Exponential Moving Average
sections.content: RMSprop fixes AdaGrad's aggressive learning rate decay by using an exponentially weighted moving average of squared gradients instead of accumulating all history. This keeps the effective learning rate from vanishing.
sections.intuition: Recent gradients matter more than ancient ones

sections.title: Adam: Adaptive Momentum
sections.content: Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) combines the best of both worlds: momentum (first moment) and adaptive learning rates (second moment). It maintains moving averages of both the gradient and its square, then applies bias correction for early iterations. Adam is the default optimizer for most deep learning—it's robust and works well across many problems with minimal tuning.
sections.recommendation: Default choice for most deep learning projects

sections.title: Adam Variants and Alternatives
sections.content: While Adam works well, researchers have developed improvements for specific scenarios. Understanding when to use each can improve your results.

variants.name: AdamW
variants.improvement: Decouples weight decay from gradient update

variants.name: AMSGrad
variants.improvement: Uses max of past v_t instead of current—ensures convergence
variants.problemSolved: Adam can fail to converge on some convex problems

variants.name: Nadam
variants.use: When you want Adam's adaptivity with Nesterov's responsiveness

sections.title: SGD with Momentum: Still Relevant
sections.content: Despite Adam's popularity, SGD with momentum often achieves better generalization (test performance) on computer vision tasks. The theory suggests that the noise in SGD acts as implicit regularization. Many state-of-the-art results use carefully tuned SGD with momentum rather than Adam.
whenToUse: When you have time to tune hyperparameters
When generalization matters more than training speed

keyConcepts.name: Second Moment
keyConcepts.description: Expected value of squared gradients—measures variance/uncertainty in gradients.
keyConcepts.usedIn: AdaGrad, RMSprop, Adam for adaptive scaling

keyConcepts.name: Bias Correction
keyConcepts.description: In Adam, initial moments are biased toward zero. Correction factor $(1-\beta^t)$ compensates.
keyConcepts.whyNeeded: Early iterations have unreliable moving averages

keyConcepts.name: Weight Decay vs L2 Regularization
keyConcepts.description: L2 regularization adds penalty to loss; weight decay subtracts from weights directly. AdamW decouples these properly.
keyConcepts.difference: Subtle but important for adaptive optimizers

keyConcepts.name: Effective Learning Rate
keyConcepts.description: The actual step size taken: $\eta_{eff} = \eta / \sqrt{v}$. Different per parameter in adaptive methods.
keyConcepts.contrast: Vanilla GD has same $\eta_{eff}$ for all parameters

complexity.memory: $O(n)$—stores 1-2 additional values per parameter (momentum, second moment)

steps.title: Vanilla SGD
steps.description: Start with basic gradient descent. All parameters use the same learning rate.

steps.title: Add Momentum
steps.description: Accumulate velocity for faster progress in consistent directions.
steps.latex: v \leftarrow \beta v + \nabla L(w), \quad w \leftarrow w - \eta v$

steps.title: AdaGrad Accumulation
steps.description: Sum squared gradients for adaptive per-parameter scaling.
steps.latex: G \leftarrow G + (\nabla L)^2, \quad w \leftarrow w - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{G}} \nabla L$

steps.title: RMSprop Smoothing
steps.description: Use exponential moving average instead of accumulation.

steps.title: Adam: Combine Both Moments
steps.description: Maintain moving averages of gradient (momentum) and squared gradient (adaptivity).

steps.title: Bias Correction
steps.description: Correct for initialization bias in early iterations.

steps.title: Final Adam Update
steps.description: Combine bias-corrected moments for the parameter update.

practiceProblems.title: AdaGrad Effective LR
practiceProblems.description: A parameter has accumulated squared gradients $G = 25$. With base LR $\eta = 0.1$, what is the effective learning rate?
practiceProblems.explanation: AdaGrad divides the learning rate by the square root of accumulated squared gradients. As gradients accumulate, the effective LR decreases.

practiceProblems.title: Adam Bias Correction
practiceProblems.description: At iteration $t=5$, raw moment estimates are $m_5 = 0.5$, $v_5 = 0.3$. With $\beta_1 = 0.9$, $\beta_2 = 0.999$, compute corrected estimates.
practiceProblems.explanation: Without correction, early estimates are biased toward 0. The correction factor $(1-\beta^t)$ grows from near 0 to 1 over time, reducing the correction magnitude.

practiceProblems.title: RMSprop vs AdaGrad
practiceProblems.description: Why does RMSprop generally outperform AdaGrad for deep learning?
practiceProblems.answer: AdaGrad's learning rate monotonically decreases and eventually becomes effectively zero, stopping learning. RMSprop's exponential moving average prevents this by 'forgetting' old gradients.
practiceProblems.explanation: In deep learning, we often need to keep learning throughout training. AdaGrad was designed for sparse convex problems (like SVMs), not deep networks where we need sustained learning.
hints: AdaGrad accumulates ALL past squared gradients

practiceProblems.title: Effective LR Comparison
practiceProblems.description: For a parameter with gradient variance: SGD has consistent gradient magnitude 1.0. Adam has $v\hat{} = 2.0$. Both use $\eta = 0.01$. Compare updates.
practiceProblems.answer: SGD update: $-0.01 \cdot 1.0 = -0.01$ | Adam update: $-0.01 \cdot m\hat{} / \sqrt{2} \approx -0.007 \cdot m\hat{}$
practiceProblems.explanation: Adam's adaptivity means it takes smaller steps when gradient variance is high. If $m\hat{} = 1$, Adam's update is ~70% of SGD's for this parameter, showing automatic step size reduction in uncertain directions.

practiceProblems.title: AdamW vs Adam
practiceProblems.description: Explain why AdamW's weight decay $\lambda\theta$ differs from Adam's L2 regularization in the gradient.
practiceProblems.answer: In Adam, L2 gradient is added before adaptive scaling, so parameters with high gradient variance get LESS regularization. In AdamW, weight decay is applied AFTER adaptive scaling, giving all parameters the same regularization strength.
practiceProblems.explanation: Adam: $g_{eff} = (g + \lambda\theta) / \sqrt{v}$—parameters with large $v$ (high variance) get suppressed regularization. AdamW: $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta(g/\sqrt{v}) - \eta\lambda\theta$—regularization independent of adaptive scaling.
hints: Consider where $\lambda\theta$ appears in the formula
Adaptive scaling affects regularization in Adam

practiceProblems.title: Optimizer Selection
practiceProblems.description: Recommend optimizers for: (a) Training BERT on text, (b) Training ResNet on ImageNet, (c) Sparse embedding learning, (d) Reinforcement learning with non-stationary gradients.
practiceProblems.answer: (a) AdamW (standard for transformers) | (b) SGD with momentum (better generalization) | (c) AdaGrad (designed for sparse gradients) | (d) RMSprop or Adam (handles changing gradients)
practiceProblems.explanation: Transformer training: AdamW is standard with weight decay for regularization. Vision: SGD often generalizes better despite slower convergence. Sparse: AdaGrad's per-parameter scaling helps rare features. RL: Non-stationary problems benefit from adaptive methods that forget old gradients.

minigame.title: Optimizer Grand Prix
minigame.description: Race different optimizers through challenging loss landscapes. See which converges fastest, which escapes saddle points, and which generalizes best.
instructions: Choose your optimizer: SGD, Momentum, AdaGrad, RMSprop, or Adam
Set hyperparameters: learning rate, momentum, betas
Navigate through valleys, avoid saddle points, find the global minimum
Compare convergence speed and final loss across optimizers
Challenge: Beat Adam with properly tuned SGD!

codeExample.code:
import numpy as np
from typing import List, Tuple

# ==================== Optimizer Implementations ====================

class Optimizer:
    """Base optimizer class"""
    def __init__(self, learning_rate=0.01):
        self.lr = learning_rate
        self.t = 0  # iteration counter
    
    def step(self, params: np.ndarray, grads: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """Update parameters and return new values"""
        raise NotImplementedError

class SGD(Optimizer):
    """Stochastic Gradient Descent"""
    def step(self, params, grads):
        self.t += 1
        return params - self.lr * grads

class SGDMomentum(Optimizer):
    """SGD with momentum"""
    def __init__(self, learning_rate=0.01, momentum=0.9):
        super().__init__(learning_rate)
        self.momentum = momentum
        self.velocity = None
    
    def step(self, params, grads):
        self.t += 1
        if self.velocity is None:
            self.velocity = np.zeros_like(params)
        
        self.velocity = self.momentum * self.velocity + self.lr * grads
        return params - self.velocity

class AdaGrad(Optimizer):
    """AdaGrad: Adaptive Gradient Algorithm"""
    def __init__(self, learning_rate=0.01, epsilon=1e-8):
        super().__init__(learning_rate)
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.accumulated = None
    
    def step(self, params, grads):
        self.t += 1
        if self.accumulated is None:
            self.accumulated = np.zeros_like(params)
        
        # Accumulate squared gradients
        self.accumulated += grads ** 2
        
        # Adaptive learning rate
        adapted_lr = self.lr / (np.sqrt(self.accumulated) + self.epsilon)
        return params - adapted_lr * grads

class RMSprop(Optimizer):
    """RMSprop: Root Mean Square Propagation"""
    def __init__(self, learning_rate=0.01, decay_rate=0.9, epsilon=1e-8):
        super().__init__(learning_rate)
        self.decay = decay_rate
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.sq_grad_ema = None
    
    def step(self, params, grads):
        self.t += 1
        if self.sq_grad_ema is None:
            self.sq_grad_ema = np.zeros_like(params)
        
        # Exponential moving average of squared gradients
        self.sq_grad_ema = self.decay * self.sq_grad_ema + (1 - self.decay) * (grads ** 2)
        
        # Adaptive update
        adapted_lr = self.lr / (np.sqrt(self.sq_grad_ema) + self.epsilon)
        return params - adapted_lr * grads

class Adam(Optimizer):
    """Adam: Adaptive Moment Estimation"""
    def __init__(self, learning_rate=0.001, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, epsilon=1e-8):
        super().__init__(learning_rate)
        self.beta1 = beta1
        self.beta2 = beta2
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.m = None  # first moment
        self.v = None  # second moment
    
    def step(self, params, grads):
        self.t += 1
        if self.m is None:
            self.m = np.zeros_like(params)
            self.v = np.zeros_like(params)
        
        # Update biased moments
        self.m = self.beta1 * self.m + (1 - self.beta1) * grads
        self.v = self.beta2 * self.v + (1 - self.beta2) * (grads ** 2)
        
        # Bias correction
        m_hat = self.m / (1 - self.beta1 ** self.t)
        v_hat = self.v / (1 - self.beta2 ** self.t)
        
        # Update
        return params - self.lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + self.epsilon)

class AdamW(Optimizer):
    """Adam with decoupled weight decay"""
    def __init__(self, learning_rate=0.001, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, epsilon=1e-8, weight_decay=0.01):
        super().__init__(learning_rate)
        self.beta1 = beta1
        self.beta2 = beta2
        self.epsilon = epsilon
        self.weight_decay = weight_decay
        self.m = None
        self.v = None
    
    def step(self, params, grads):
        self.t += 1
        if self.m is None:
            self.m = np.zeros_like(params)
            self.v = np.zeros_like(params)
        
        # Adam update on gradients
        self.m = self.beta1 * self.m + (1 - self.beta1) * grads
        self.v = self.beta2 * self.v + (1 - self.beta2) * (grads ** 2)
        
        m_hat = self.m / (1 - self.beta1 ** self.t)
        v_hat = self.v / (1 - self.beta2 ** self.t)
        
        # Decoupled weight decay
        params_adam = params - self.lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + self.epsilon)
        return params_adam - self.lr * self.weight_decay * params

# ==================== Comparison and Testing ====================

def compare_optimizers(func, grad_func, x0, iterations=1000):
    """
    Compare all optimizers on a test function
    Returns: dict of optimizer name -> (trajectory, losses)
    """
    optimizers = {
        'SGD': SGD(learning_rate=0.1),
        'SGD+Momentum': SGDMomentum(learning_rate=0.1, momentum=0.9),
        'AdaGrad': AdaGrad(learning_rate=0.1),
        'RMSprop': RMSprop(learning_rate=0.1, decay_rate=0.9),
        'Adam': Adam(learning_rate=0.1, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999),
        'AdamW': AdamW(learning_rate=0.1, weight_decay=0.01)
    }
    
    results = {}
    
    for name, opt in optimizers.items():
        x = x0.copy()
        trajectory = [x.copy()]
        losses = [func(x)]
        
        for _ in range(iterations):
            grad = grad_func(x)
            x = opt.step(x, grad)
            trajectory.append(x.copy())
            losses.append(func(x))
        
        results[name] = (np.array(trajectory), np.array(losses))
    
    return results

def rosenbrock(x):
    """Rosenbrock function - optimization test"""
    return (1 - x[0])**2 + 100 * (x[1] - x[0]**2)**2

def rosenbrock_grad(x):
    dx0 = -2*(1 - x[0]) - 400*x[0]*(x[1] - x[0]**2)
    dx1 = 200*(x[1] - x[0]**2)
    return np.array([dx0, dx1])

# Test
if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Optimizer Comparison on Rosenbrock ===")
    x0 = np.array([-1.0, 2.0])
    
    results = compare_optimizers(rosenbrock, rosenbrock_grad, x0, iterations=2000)
    
    print(f"\nStarting point: {x0}")
    print(f"Global minimum: [1, 1] with loss 0\n")
    
    for name, (traj, losses) in results.items():
        final_x = traj[-1]
        final_loss = losses[-1]
        print(f"{name:15s}: final x = [{final_x[0]:8.4f}, {final_x[1]:8.4f}], loss = {final_loss:.6f}")
    
    print("\n=== Effective Learning Rate Analysis ===")
    # Sparse gradient scenario
    grad_sparse = np.array([0.001, 10.0])  # very different magnitudes
    
    ada = AdaGrad(learning_rate=0.1)
    ada.accumulated = np.array([100.0, 0.1])  # simulated history
    
    effective_lr_ada = ada.lr / (np.sqrt(ada.accumulated) + ada.epsilon)
    print(f"AdaGrad effective LRs: {effective_lr_ada}")
    print(f"→ Rare feature LR: {effective_lr_ada[0]:.4f}, Frequent feature LR: {effective_lr_ada[1]:.4f}")
    print(f"→ AdaGrad gives larger updates to rarely updated parameters!")
